interactions.summary: Jiang corrects the class's chronology by distinguishing Augustus from Tiberius, then ties Augustus to Jesus's birth and to the imperial conditions that allowed Christianity to arise.

A student suggests Dante dislikes Augustus for instrumentalizing Virgil and piety, and Jiang radicalizes that answer into a claim that Augustus corrupted divine poetry for empire and was therefore erased beyond hell itself.

speaker_notes.note: These are empty or overlapping diarization fragments and do not carry semantic content.

claims.claim: Jiang corrects the class by saying Jesus was killed under Tiberius, not Augustus.
Jiang says Jesus was born during Augustus and that Catholic teaching treats Augustus's empire as part of the worldly pathway that made Christianity possible.
A student suggests Dante may dislike Augustus because Augustus turned Virgil and piety toward imperial service.
Jiang says poetry is the greatest act of faith, love, and hope because Virgil is a divine prophet-poet, and Augustus's crime was to corrupt that divine gift to serve imperial politics.
Jiang argues that Augustus is not merely damned but cast to a place worse than hell, namely annihilation and divine forgetting beyond the universe.
Jiang says the greatest crime in the world is to corrupt God's message for one's own political ends.

signature_moments.moment: Augustus is assigned not to hell but to annihilation beyond Dante's universe.
signature_moments.source_phrase: a place worse than hell. Which is annihilation
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's most extreme Jiang move and turns absence into the harshest possible judgment.

signature_moments.moment: Empire corrupts divine poetry by forcing it to serve politics.
signature_moments.source_phrase: He corrupted it to serve the ends of empire
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It crystallizes Jiang's larger suspicion that sacred or imaginative technologies become monstrous when annexed by power.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's term for a punishment beyond hell itself, where Augustus is forgotten by God rather than merely tormented.
Jiang's description of Virgil as a poet whose gift carries divine authority and therefore becomes especially dangerous when used for empire.

chronology_notes.note: The packet first cleans up Roman-Christian chronology and then converts the Augustus puzzle into Jiang's strongest anti-imperial reading so far in the lecture.

uncertainty_notes.note: The student's wording about piety and Augustus is ASR-rough, but the gist is that Augustus instrumentalizes Virgil and imperial ideology.
